steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the History section of a Wikipedia-style article on the Atari Portfolio, covering how it came out of DIP Research's palmtop design, how Atari licensed and marketed it, and what became of DIP.

steps.text:
DIP Research Ltd. was a company at the Surrey Research Park in Guildford, Surrey, UK, and it developed the DIP Pocket PC, which was the first palmtop PC that was MS-DOS-compatible. It was compatible with the IBM PC at the BIOS level, but it was not compatible at the I/O port level. In early 1989 a prototype version was released as a proof of concept.

Atari found out about this release and saw that there was a market opportunity. Atari licensed the electronics and software design from DIP, and then used its production engineering expertise to make a consumer version of the product, which had a new case and a new keyboard.

- Names by country
  - marketed as Atari Portfolio in US & UK, other countries later
  - Germany, Italy, Spain: initially PC Folio (trademark restrictions)
  - Atari later acquired Portfolio name in Germany and Spain; always PC Folio in Italy
- DIP's continued role
  - kept evolving electronics (incl. expansion modules) and all ROM software, updates to Atari over production cycle
  - licensing deal: DIP sourced Portfolios at reduced cost -> rebranded, sold as production DIP Pocket PC in UK
  - note Atari key on keyboard
- Later
  - Sharp PC-3000/3100, late 1991
  - acquired by Phoenix Technologies 1994
  - name: Distributed Information Processing officially; unofficially founders' initials (David Frodsham, Ian Cullimore, Peter Baldwin)
  - founders and several staff previously at Psion (company)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
DIP Research Ltd. was a company at the Surrey Research Park in Guildford, Surrey, UK, and it developed the DIP Pocket PC, which was the first palmtop PC that was MS-DOS-compatible. It was compatible with the IBM PC at the BIOS level, but it was not compatible at the I/O port level. In early 1989 a prototype version was released as a proof of concept.

Atari found out about this release and saw that there was a market opportunity. Atari licensed the electronics and software design from DIP, and then used its production engineering expertise to make a consumer version of the product, which had a new case and a new keyboard.

The product was marketed as the Atari Portfolio in the US and the UK, and later on in other countries too. In Germany, Italy and Spain it was called the PC Folio at first, because of trademark restrictions. Later Atari acquired the rights to the Portfolio name in Germany and Spain, but in Italy it was always called the PC Folio.

DIP kept on developing the electronics design, including expansion modules, and also all of the ROM software, and it supplied software updates to Atari during the production cycle. Because of the licensing agreement DIP could get Portfolios from Atari at a reduced cost, and it rebranded these and sold them in the UK as the production version of the DIP Pocket PC. The Atari key is still on the keyboard.

DIP Research also developed the Sharp PC-3000/3100, which came out in late 1991. Phoenix Technologies acquired the company in 1994.

The name DIP officially stood for Distributed Information Processing, but unofficially it was the initials of the founders, David Frodsham, Ian Cullimore and Peter Baldwin. Before they founded DIP, the founders and several staff members had worked at Psion (company).

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
DIP Research Ltd., based at the Surrey Research Park in Guildford, Surrey, UK, developed the first MS-DOS-compatible palmtop PC, the DIP Pocket PC. It was IBM PC-compatible at the BIOS level, though not at the I/O port level. A prototype version was released in early 1989 as a proof of concept.

Atari became aware of this release and saw a market opportunity. It licensed the electronics and software design from DIP, and applied its production engineering expertise to create a consumer version of the product with a new case and keyboard.

This product was marketed[1] as the Atari Portfolio in the US and UK, and later in other countries. In Germany, Italy, and Spain it was initially called the PC Folio[2] because of trademark restrictions. Atari acquired the rights to the Portfolio name in Germany and Spain, but in Italy it was always called the PC Folio.

DIP continued to evolve the electronics design (including expansion modules) and all the ROM software, supplying software updates to Atari throughout the production cycle. Its licensing agreement let it source Portfolios from Atari at a reduced cost, which it rebranded and sold in the UK as the production version of the DIP Pocket PC[3]. Note the Atari key on the keyboard.

DIP Research also developed the Sharp PC-3000/3100, released in late 1991. The company was acquired by Phoenix Technologies in 1994.

Officially the name DIP stood for Distributed Information Processing; unofficially it was the initials of the founders David Frodsham, Ian Cullimore and Peter Baldwin.

Before founding DIP, the founders and several staff members had worked at Psion (company).

References:
[1] Atari Corporation. (1990). Atari Portfolio Brochure. http://archive.org/details/AtariPortfolioBrochure1990
[2] Atari PC Folio. http://www.atari-computermuseum.de/pics/scans/pcfolio_0289.pdf
[3] Ordric. (2011-04-11). English: Image of a production DIP Pocket PC - Essentially a rebranded Atari Portfolio. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:100_4868.JPG
